openingMessage: The most important thing a leader can do is create an environment where everyone feels they are part of the team and the team is part of them.
openingWhy: The hand who feels like an outsider won't call stop-work — he'll hope somebody senior does it first. The crew where the greenest worm will grab an operator's sleeve and say 'walk me through this' is the crew that catches what everybody else walks right past.
leadershipThought: Act like a professional at all times. Respect the environment. Be aware. Don't create distractions. Act like the person the client would want back tomorrow.

specialFocus.title: Core Values — On Time, and Out of the Truck
specialFocus.why: These aren't policies and they aren't suggestions — they're who Canon is. A company man plans his whole morning around when we say we'll be there: crews stage, work holds, and the clock starts on our word. And once we're on location, our value isn't the seat of a truck — it's a second set of eyes in the work. Two core values, one message: show up when you said, and be all the way there when you do.
specialFocus.standardLabel: The Standard — Core Values, Not Options
standard: Be on time — every location, every day. On time is fundamental to Canon Safety. The crew that's waiting on us can't break containment without us, and every minute they wait is our name on the delay.

Can't make it on time? The call is a MUST. The moment you know you'll be late — traffic, breakdown, held at the yard — you call, so we can inform the company man before he's looking at an empty gate. Late with a call ahead is a plan the location can work around. Late without one is a no-show until the second you arrive.

Get out of your truck and be involved. Park it, walk the location, find the PIC, ask what's moving today. Your task being done doesn't mean you're done — 'I'm here to help, what can I do?' is the Canon handshake. Nobody protects a location through a windshield.

scenarios.title: Twenty Minutes Out at Five Till
scenarios.body: It's 5:40 AM, the job starts at 6:00, and you're twenty minutes past that on your best day — wreck on the highway, nothing you did wrong. The temptation is to push hard and slip in quiet, hoping nobody clocks it. The standard is the opposite: make the call NOW, while the news is still useful. Dispatch tells the company man, he re-sequences his morning, and when you roll in he already knows — Canon's word held even when the road didn't. Then finish it right: park, get out, walk to the crew, and get in the work. The late arrival people forget; the empty gate and the tech who never left the cab, they remember.

questions: You're going to be fifteen minutes late tomorrow — who do you call, and do you have that number in your phone right now?
When your task is done and the crew is still working, where are you standing — and what does the company man see when he looks over?
What time do you have to leave the yard to be EARLY to your farthest location — not on time, early?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: On time, or on the phone before you're late — so the company man hears it from us, not from an empty gate. And out of the truck, in the work. These are core values. This is who we are.
